attacks.claim: Nightly job scores all 340k recipes for every pantry user in one SQL statement. At 30% of 2.1M MAU (~630k pantry users), that is roughly 2 x 10^11 user-recipe pairs per run, versus the staging benchmark of 12,000 users in 41 minutes (~50x more users, so the job would need days, not minutes). It will overrun the 02:00 UTC window and contend with the primary.
attacks.evidence: "Staging run: 12,000 synthetic pantry users completed in 41 minutes." / "Adoption assumption for sizing: 30% of MAU create a pantry within 90 days."

attacks.claim: A single monolithic statement joining pantry_items x recipe_ingredients on the primary, run nightly for all users, has no batching, timeout, or partial-failure plan. A failure mid-run leaves pantry_matches stale or half-upserted, and the plan names no alerting or runtime budget.
attacks.evidence: "score every recipe in the catalog (340k recipes) in a single SQL statement joining pantry_items x recipe_ingredients on the primary"

attacks.claim: The job reads and writes the primary while the 78% US-time-zone user base is active at 02:00 UTC (evening in US). Replicas are not mentioned for the read-heavy scoring query, so the job competes with live traffic on the primary.
attacks.evidence: "joining pantry_items x recipe_ingredients on the primary"

attacks.claim: The plan requires expiry dates for the unlock count, but the scoring formula weights by expiry proximity and the notification depends on expiry. Items without expiry dates (common for pantry staples and shelf-stable goods) are counted toward the 15-item unlock yet have no defined score weight, so the behaviour for them is unspecified.
attacks.evidence: "unlocks once a user has entered at least 15 items with expiry dates" / "weighted by expiry proximity"

attacks.claim: Staples are 'always counted as present', which inflates scores for recipes that are mostly staples and can make a recipe with few real pantry matches rank highly. The formula's denominator and handling of zero-ingredient matches are not defined.
attacks.evidence: "with pantry staples (salt, oil, water, pepper) always counted as present"

attacks.claim: The core hypothesis (reason #2 'ingredients I don't have' is solved by matching what users already own) and the 25% unlock target rest on an unvalidated 30% pantry-adoption assumption and a 15-item gate that was never tested. The 15-item threshold, a load-bearing product choice, has no cited evidence, and no prototype or user test is referenced.
attacks.evidence: "Adoption assumption for sizing: 30% of MAU create a pantry within 90 days." / "To keep match quality high, Pantry Match unlocks once a user has entered at least 15 items"

attacks.claim: The plan targets exit reason #1 (too much setup/typing, 38%) yet the core feature requires users to type 15 items with expiry dates before any value appears. That is a larger setup burden than the one that drove churn, and the plan does not address it.
attacks.evidence: "Users add items with a form: ingredient (autocomplete over our 9,400-ingredient catalog), quantity, unit, expiry date." / "Until then the tab shows a progress bar"

attacks.claim: Post-cook quantity updates add recurring friction on the recipe screen; the plan does not say how the pantry stays accurate if users skip the prompt, which undermines match quality.
attacks.evidence: "Users are asked to update quantities after cooking (prompt on the recipe 'I made this' screen)."

attacks.claim: Pantry contents and expiry data are personal behavioural data (what users keep at home, and when they cook). The plan has no retention, deletion, or consent language beyond the push opt-in.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention and deletion policy for pantry_items and pantry_matches

attacks.claim: Launch is a 5%-then-100% rollout within week 6, with no stated rollback or kill switch for the nightly job or the carousel.
Nightly full-catalog scoring for hundreds of thousands of users has no compute budget estimate, so cost at scale is unknown.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: compute or cost estimate for PantryMatchJob

attacks.claim: Progress bar and carousel have no stated accessibility requirements (screen reader labels, contrast, motion).
attacks.evidence: "the tab shows a progress bar ("7 of 15 items added")"

attacks.claim: The 6-week schedule puts scoring, job, and carousel in weeks 3-4 across four engineers and three platforms with no slack and no load test at production scale.
